adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
adds.summary: The national-framework page under which a visitor to Cross River stands: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide, and the Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — carry up to a death-penalty maximum, and Cross River is not among them, matching the record's claim. The page documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023), with no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Confirms every national-framework element the record asserts for this state: the 14-year ceiling, exclusion from the sharia death-penalty regime, kito/gang risk and enforcement pattern.

adds.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents the abuse pattern this record attributes to law enforcement: arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones; the report is national in scope and does not name Cross River. It substantiates the record's national baseline that police treat suspected same-sex conduct and perceived 'gayness' as an extortion opportunity, with release on payment of a bribe as the documented outcome.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
adds.summary: National-framework source applicable to Oyo: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). The twelve Shari'a-law states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — carry up to a death-penalty maximum for male same-sex conduct; Oyo is a southern state outside that regime, as the record states. The page documents that police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito') and that mass arrests recur across states (42 men arrested in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023), with no anti-discrimination protections. Supports the record's claims that the 2014 statute also reaches LGBTI organisations and that LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under the framework that applies in full to Oyo.

adds.title: The Nigerians lured into a trap and blackmailed for being gay (BBC News / BBC Africa Eye)
adds.summary: BBC Africa Eye's 15 May 2023 investigation by Ian Wafula and Tamasin Ford documents the 'kito' scheme the record warns about: criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular dating apps, entrap men, film them, and then extort, beat and even kidnap them, with the investigation interviewing 21 people about being 'kito'd'. Victims do not report to police for fear of being arrested or attacked, and the piece shows police-adjacent enforcement against the gangs, including a commander quoted as vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. National in scope (the underground scene described is Lagos-based), it substantiates the record's point that dating-app 'kito' extortion gangs are a nationwide risk for gay and transgender app users, a risk that applies in Oyo exactly as elsewhere in the country.
